dhpak1.2:1.1: 1. The Chapter about the Pairs Yamakavagga
dhpak1.2:2.1: 1.1 The Story about the Elder Cakkhupāla Cakkhupālattheravatthu
dhpak1.2:3.1: Mind precedes thoughts, mind is their chief, {1.3} [28.146] their quality is made by mind,
dhpak1.2:3.2: if with base mind one speaks or acts
dhpak1.2:3.3: through that suffering follows one like a wheel follows ox’s foot.
dhpak1.2:4.1: Where was this Dhamma teaching given? At Sāvatthī. With reference to whom? The Elder Cakkhupāla.
dhpak1.2:5.1: At Sāvatthī, we are told, lived a householder named Mahā Suvaṇṇa (Great Gold).
dhpak1.2:5.2: He was rich, possessed of great wealth, possessed of ample means of enjoyment, but at the same time he was childless.
dhpak1.2:5.3: One day, as he was on his way home from bathing at a river, he saw by the roadside a large forest tree with spreading branches.
dhpak1.2:5.4: He thought: “This tree must be tenanted by a powerful Devatā.”
dhpak1.2:5.5: So he caused the ground under the tree to be cleared, the tree itself to be enclosed with a wall, and sand to be spread within the enclosure.
dhpak1.2:5.6: And having decked the tree with flags and banners, he made the following vow:
dhpak1.2:5.7: “Should I obtain a son or a daughter, I will pay you great honor.”
dhpak1.2:5.8: Having so done, he went on his way.
dhpak1.2:6.1: Now, in no long time his wife conceived a child in her womb.
dhpak1.2:6.2: {1.4} So soon as his wife knew that she was with child, she informed her husband, and he performed the protection of the womb for her.
dhpak1.2:6.3: On the expiration of ten lunar months she gave birth to a son.
dhpak1.2:6.4: Since the merchant obtained a son by protecting the tree, he named his son Pāla (Protector).
dhpak1.2:7.1: After a time he obtained a second son.
dhpak1.2:7.2: The younger son he named Culla Pāla (Protector Junior), calling the older son Mahā Pāla (Protector Senior).
dhpak1.2:7.3: When they reached manhood, their parents obtained wives for them.
dhpak1.2:7.4: After a time the mother and father died, leaving the entire estate to be administered by the two sons.
dhpak1.2:8.1: At this time the Teacher, having set in motion the glorious Wheel of the Dhamma,
dhpak1.2:8.2: after journeying from place to place, took up his residence at Jetavana,
dhpak1.2:8.3: a monastery erected by the wealthy merchant [28.147] Anāthapiṇḍika at a cost of 540 millions coins.
dhpak1.2:8.4: While in residence at Jetavana, he established the multitude in the way to heaven and the way to deliverance.
dhpak1.2:9.1: For the Realised One kept residence during but a single rainy season at the monastery erected by twice 80,000 families of kinsmen,
dhpak1.2:9.2: eighty on his mother’s side and eighty on his father’s.
dhpak1.2:9.3: At Jetavana monastery, erected by Anāthapiṇḍika, he kept residence during nineteen rainy seasons;
dhpak1.2:9.4: at Pubbārāma, erected by Visākhā at a cost of 270 milllion, he kept residence during six rainy seasons.
dhpak1.2:9.5: Thus, by reason of the great merit of these two families,
dhpak1.2:9.6: he kept residence near Sāvatthī during twenty-five rainy seasons.
dhpak1.2:10.1: Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, the eminent female lay disciple, regularly went twice every day to wait upon the Realised One.
dhpak1.2:10.2: Knowing that the young novices would expect alms from them, they never went empty-handed.
dhpak1.2:10.3: Before breakfast {1.5} they took food, both hard and soft;
dhpak1.2:10.4: after breakfast they took the five medicaments and the eight beverages.
dhpak1.2:10.5: Moreover, in their residences seats were always prepared for two thousand bhikkhus.
dhpak1.2:10.6: Whoever wished food or drink or medicine was immediately provided with just what he wished.
dhpak1.2:11.1: However, not a single day had Anāthapiṇḍika asked the Teacher a question.
dhpak1.2:11.2: Anāthapiṇḍika, we are told, refrained from asking questions by reason of his excessive love for the Teacher.
dhpak1.2:11.3: He thought to himself: “The Realised One is a delicate Buddha, a delicate prince.
dhpak1.2:11.4: Were the Teacher, because of the thought: ‘This householder is my supporter,’ to teach the Dhamma to me, he would grow weary.”
dhpak1.2:11.5: Therefore he asked the Teacher no questions.
dhpak1.2:11.6: But so soon as Anāthapiṇḍika took his seat, the Teacher thought to himself: “This merchant protects me where I have no need to be protected.
dhpak1.2:11.7: For I spent four immeasurables and 100,000 aeons of time in addition fulfilling the perfections.
dhpak1.2:11.8: My own gloriously adorned head have I cut off; my eyes have I torn out; my heart’s flesh have I uprooted;
dhpak1.2:11.9: both son and wife, dear to me as life, have I renounced, solely that I might teach the Dhamma to others.
dhpak1.2:11.10: This man protects me where I have no need to be protected.” And straightaway he taught a sermon on the Dhamma.
dhpak1.2:12.1: At this time seventy million people dwelt in Sāvatthī.
dhpak1.2:12.2: Of these, fifty million became noble disciples after hearing the discourse of the Teacher, but twenty million remained unattained.
dhpak1.2:12.3: The noble disciples had two duties: before breakfast they gave alms;
dhpak1.2:12.4: after breakfast, bearing perfumes and garlands in their hands,
dhpak1.2:12.5: with [28.148] servants bearing garments, medicaments, and beverages, they went to hear the Dhamma.
dhpak1.2:13.1: Now one day Mahā Pāla saw the noble disciples going to the monastery with perfumes and garlands in their hands.
dhpak1.2:13.2: {1.6} When he saw them, he asked: “Where is this great throng going?”
dhpak1.2:13.3: – “To hear the Dhamma.” – “I will go too,” he said.
dhpak1.2:13.4: So he went, worshipped the Teacher, and sat down in the outer circle of the congregation.
dhpak1.2:14.1: Now when the Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they have regard to the predispositions of their hearers for the refuges, the moral precepts, and going forth.
dhpak1.2:14.2: Thus they always teach the Dhamma with reference to the disposition of mind of each individual.
dhpak1.2:14.3: When, therefore, the Teacher taught the Dhamma on that day, he had regard to Mahā Pāla’s predispositions.
dhpak1.2:14.4: And he taught in orderly sequence, expounding one subject after another;
dhpak1.2:14.5: to wit, almsgiving, the moral precepts, heaven, the dangers of sensual pleasures,
dhpak1.2:14.6: the baseness of the defilments, and the advantages of going forth.
dhpak1.2:15.2: He thought: “When a man goes to the next world, neither sons nor daughters nor riches follow him; nay, even his own body does not go with him.
dhpak1.2:15.3: Of what profit is it for me to live the household life? I will go forth.”
dhpak1.2:15.4: So at the end of the discourse he approached the Teacher and asked to be given the going forth.
dhpak1.2:15.5: The Teacher asked him: “Have you no kinsman of whom it is proper that you should ask leave?”
dhpak1.2:15.6: – “Why yes, venerable Sir, I have a younger brother.” – “Well then, ask him.”
dhpak1.2:15.7: To this Mahā Pāla agreed, and said: “Very well.” So he worshipped the Teacher and went home.
dhpak1.2:16.1: Summoning his younger brother, he said to him:
dhpak1.2:16.2: “Dear brother, whatever wealth is in this house, whether animate or inanimate, all this I give into your hands; take possession thereof.”
dhpak1.2:16.3: – “But you, master?” – “I shall go forth under the Teacher.”
dhpak1.2:16.4: – “What say you, dear brother? When my mother died, I gained in you as it were a mother;
dhpak1.2:16.5: when my father died, as it were a father. Your house contains great wealth.
dhpak1.2:16.6: Surely you can do works of merit even though you live the household life. {1.7} Do not so.”
dhpak1.2:16.7: – “Dear brother, after hearing the Teacher teach the Dhamma, I can no longer live the life of a householder.
dhpak1.2:16.8: For the Teacher taught a Dhamma lovely in its beginning, its middle, and its end,
dhpak1.2:16.9: and established precisely and exactly the three characteristics of existing things: impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
dhpak1.2:16.10: I cannot fulfill the Dhamma amid the [28.149] cares of the household life; I must go forth, dear brother.”
dhpak1.2:16.11: – “Dear brother, now you are young. Wait until you are old, and then go forth.”
dhpak1.2:16.12: – “Dear brother, in the case of an old man, even hands and feet are disobedient and do not answer to his will; how much more so his kinsmen?
dhpak1.2:16.13: No, I will not do as you say; I will fulfill the duties of a bhikkhu.
dhpak1.2:17.1: Weakened by old age are hands and feet, disobedient.
dhpak1.2:17.2: For the one lacking strength how will he live by the Dhamma?
dhpak1.2:18.1: Dear brother, I shall go forth despite all considerations to the contrary.”
dhpak1.2:19.1: In spite of his brother’s lamentations Mahā Pāla went to the Teacher and asked to go forth.
dhpak1.2:19.2: He went forth and took higher ordination and spent five rainy seasons in residence with his teachers and preceptor.
dhpak1.2:19.3: When he had completed his fifth residence and celebrated the Invitation, he approached the Teacher, worshipped him, and asked:
dhpak1.2:19.4: “Venerable Sir, how many duties are there in this religion?”
dhpak1.2:19.5: – “Two duties only, bhikkhu: the duty of study and the duty of meditation.”
dhpak1.2:19.6: – “Venerable Sir, what is meant by the duty of study, and what is meant by the duty of meditation?”
dhpak1.2:19.7: – “The duty of study necessitates gaining a knowledge of the word of the Buddha in a manner conformable to one’s understanding,
dhpak1.2:19.8: the mastery of one or two Collections (Nikāya), or indeed of the whole Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka), bearing it in mind, reciting it, teaching it.
dhpak1.2:19.9: {1.8} On the other hand the duty of meditation, which leads to Arahatship, involves frugal living,
dhpak1.2:19.10: satisfaction with a remote lodging, fixing firmly in one’s mind the idea of decay and death,
dhpak1.2:19.11: and the development of insight by persistent effort.”
dhpak1.2:19.12: – “Venerable Sir, since I went forth in old age, I shall not be able to fulfill the duty of study.
dhpak1.2:19.13: But I can fulfill the duty of meditation; teach me a meditation subject.”
dhpak1.2:20.1: So the Teacher taught him a meditation subject leading to Arahatship.
dhpak1.2:20.2: Then he worshipped the Teacher, sought bhikkhus to accompany him, and having obtained sixty, departed with them.
dhpak1.2:20.3: When he had proceeded a distance of twenty leagues, he arrived at a large border-village, and accompanied by his retinue, entered the village for alms.
dhpak1.2:20.4: The inhabitants, observing that the bhikkhus were faithful in the performance of their duties,
dhpak1.2:20.5: were favorably disposed to them, provided them with seats, and served them with savoury food.
dhpak1.2:20.6: Then they enquired: “Venerable Sirs, where do the noble bhikkhus go?”
dhpak1.2:20.8: Then the wise villagers knew [28.150] within themselves: “The venerable bhikkhus seek lodgings wherein to spend the rainy season.”
dhpak1.2:21.1: They said: “If the noble bhikkhus would reside here during these three months, we would abide steadfast in the refuges and receive the moral precepts.”
dhpak1.2:21.2: The bhikkhus, thinking to themselves: “Through these families we shall effect escape from the round of existences,” gave their consent.
dhpak1.2:21.3: The villagers, having obtained the consent of the bhikkhus, proceeded to erect a monastery,
dhpak1.2:21.4: building night-quarters and day-quarters, and when it was finished, presented it to the bhikkhus.
dhpak1.2:21.5: The bhikkhus resorted regularly to that village only for alms.
dhpak1.2:21.6: And a certain physician came to them and offered his services, saying:
dhpak1.2:21.7: “Venerable Sirs, where many reside, disease is inevitable.
dhpak1.2:21.8: Should sickness arise, pray send me word, and I will prescribe remedies for you.”
dhpak1.2:22.1: When the bhikkhus entered upon residence on the first day of the rainy season, the elder, addressing them, asked this question:
dhpak1.2:22.2: {1.9} “Friends, in how many postures will you spend these three months?”
dhpak1.2:22.3: – “In all four postures, venerable Sir.” – “But, friends, is this proper?
dhpak1.2:22.4: Assuredly we must be heedful, for it was from the living Buddha that we received our meditation subject on coming here;
dhpak1.2:22.5: and the favor of the Buddhas may not be won by double-dealing, but only by the manifestation of upright intent.
dhpak1.2:22.6: Four states of suffering await he who is heedless, that he may enter therein as into his own habitation.
dhpak1.2:22.7: Therefore, friends, be heedful.” – “But you, venerable Sir?”
dhpak1.2:22.8: – “I shall spend the time in the three postures; I shall not stretch out my back, friends.”
dhpak1.2:23.1: A Vow of Heedfulness At the end of the first month the elder, who allowed himself no sleep, began to suffer from an affliction of the eyes.
dhpak1.2:23.2: Streams of tears trickled from his eyes, as streams of water from a broken jar.
dhpak1.2:23.3: All night long he devoted himself to meditation, and with the coming of dawn he entered his cell and sat down.
dhpak1.2:23.4: When it was time for the bhikkhus to go the rounds for alms, they came to the elder and said to him:
dhpak1.2:23.5: “Venerable Sir, it is time for us to go the rounds for alms.” – “Very well, friends; take bowl and robe.”
dhpak1.2:23.6: Having thus directed them to take their own bowls and robes, he himself set out.
dhpak1.2:23.7: The bhikkhus observed that his eyes were running and asked him: “What is the matter, venerable Sir?”
dhpak1.2:23.8: – “The wind cuts my eyes, friends.” – “Were we not offered the services of a physician, venerable Sir?
dhpak1.2:23.9: We will inform him.” – “Very well, {1.10} friends.” [28.151]
dhpak1.2:24.1: They informed the physician, who prepared an ointment and sent it to the elder.
dhpak1.2:24.2: The elder applied the ointment, remaining seated as he did so, and then entered the village.
dhpak1.2:24.3: The physician, seeing him, said to him: “Venerable Sir, I am informed that the wind hurts your reverence’s eyes.”
dhpak1.2:24.4: – “That is true, lay disciple.” – “Venerable Sir, did you apply an ointment which I prepared and sent you?”
dhpak1.2:24.5: – “Yes, lay disciple.” – “How do you feel now?”
dhpak1.2:24.6: – “The pain continues just the same, lay disciple.”
dhpak1.2:24.7: The physician thought to himself: “The ointment which I sent him should have cured him with only one application.
dhpak1.2:24.8: How is it that he is not cured?” So he asked the elder: “Were you seated when you applied the ointment, or were you lying down?”
dhpak1.2:24.9: The elder remained silent. Though the physician repeated the question several times, he answered not a word.
dhpak1.2:24.10: The physician thought to himself: “I will go to the monastery and have a look at his cell.”
dhpak1.2:24.11: So he dismissed the elder, saying to him: “That will do, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.2:25.1: Going to the monastery, he inspected the elder’s cell.
dhpak1.2:25.2: Seeing only a place to walk and a place to sit down, but no place to lie down, he asked the elder:
dhpak1.2:25.3: “Venerable Sir, were you seated when you applied the ointment, or were you lying down?” The elder remained silent.
dhpak1.2:25.4: “Venerable Sir, do not act in this way; the duties of a religious can be performed only so long as the body is properly cared for.
dhpak1.2:25.5: Were you lying down when you applied the ointment?”
dhpak1.2:25.6: After the physician had repeated the question several times, the elder replied:
dhpak1.2:25.7: “Go your way, friend; I will take counsel and decide the matter for myself.”
dhpak1.2:26.1: Now the elder had no kinsmen or blood-relatives there. With whom, therefore, was he to take counsel?
dhpak1.2:26.2: Therefore he took counsel with his own person, saying: {1.11} “Come now, brother Pālita, tell me this.
dhpak1.2:26.3: Will you give regard to your eyes or to the dispensation of the Buddha?
dhpak1.2:26.4: For in the round of existences without conceivable beginning, there is no counting the number of times you have been without eyes.
dhpak1.2:26.5: But while unnumbered hundreds of Buddhas and thousands of Buddhas have passed, your experience does not cover the period of even a single Buddha.
dhpak1.2:26.6: Now in this rainy season you resolved not to lie down for three months.
dhpak1.2:26.7: Therefore let your eyes perish or decay. Keep only the dispensation of the Buddha, not your eyes.”
dhpak1.2:26.8: And admonishing his own physical body, he uttered the following verses:
dhpak1.2:27.2: my ears decline, and likewise also my body;
dhpak1.2:27.3: all that depends on the body declines
dhpak1.2:28.2: my ears decay, and likewise also my body;
dhpak1.2:28.3: all that depends on the body decays
dhpak1.2:29.2: my ears will fail, and likewise also my body;
dhpak1.2:29.3: all that depends on the body will fail
dhpak1.2:30.1: Having thus admonished himself in three verses, he applied the ointment to his nose, remaining seated as before, and then entered the village for alms.
dhpak1.2:30.2: The physician, seeing him, asked him: “Venerable Sir, have you applied the ointment?”
dhpak1.2:30.4: – “The pain continues just the same, lay disciple.”
dhpak1.2:30.5: – “Venerable Sir, were you seated when you applied the ointment, or were you lying down?”
dhpak1.2:30.6: The elder remained silent. The physician repeated the question several times, but the elder answered never a word.
dhpak1.2:30.7: Then the physician said to him: “You are not doing as you ought for your own good.
dhpak1.2:30.8: Henceforth do not say: ‘So and So prepared ointment for me’ and I will not say: ‘I prepared ointment for you.’”
dhpak1.2:31.1: Given up on by the physician, the elder went to the monastery.
dhpak1.2:31.2: He said: “Bhikkhu, though you have been given up by the physician, do not give up your posture.
dhpak1.2:32.1: Being refused medicine, rejected by the doctor,
dhpak1.2:32.2: destined for the King of Death, why, Pālita, be heedless?
dhpak1.2:33.1: Having admonished himself in this verse, he resumed his meditations.
dhpak1.2:33.2: At the end of the middle watch his eyes and his pollutants were blotted out simultaneously,
dhpak1.2:33.3: and he became an Arahat through pure insight. He entered his cell and sat down.
dhpak1.2:34.1: Blindness and Insight When the time came for the bhikkhus to go the rounds for alms, they came to the elder and said to him:
dhpak1.2:34.2: “Venerable Sir, it is time for us to go the rounds for alms.” – “Is it time, friends?”
dhpak1.2:34.3: – “Yes, venerable Sir.” – “Well then, go your way.” – “But you, venerable Sir?”
dhpak1.2:34.4: – “The sight of my eyes is gone, friends.” They looked at his eyes, and their own eyes filled with tears.
dhpak1.2:34.5: “Do not worry, venerable Sir; {1.13} we will look after you,” they said to the elder, comforting him.
dhpak1.2:34.6: And having performed the various duties required of them, they entered the village for alms.
dhpak1.2:35.1: Not seeing the elder, people asked the bhikkhus: “Friends, where is our noble elder?”
dhpak1.2:35.2: When they learned what had happened, they sent rice-porridge to him.
dhpak1.2:35.3: Afterwards, taking food, they went in person, [28.153] worshipped the elder, and rolling on the ground before his feet, poured out their lamentations.
dhpak1.2:35.4: Then they comforted him, saying: “We will care for you, venerable Sir; do not worry,” and went their way.
dhpak1.2:35.5: From that time on they sent rice-porridge regularly to the monastery.
dhpak1.2:36.1: The elder constantly admonished the other sixty bhikkhus, and they carried out his admonitions so faithfully that at
dhpak1.2:36.2: the approaching Invitation (Pavāraṇā) all of them became Arahats possessed of the analytic knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
dhpak1.2:36.3: At the end of the rainy season, desiring to see the Teacher, they said to the elder:
dhpak1.2:36.4: “Venerable Sir, we desire to see the Teacher.”
dhpak1.2:36.5: When the elder heard their request, he thought to himself:
dhpak1.2:36.6: “I am weak, and on the way is a forest haunted by Amanussa (Non-Human Beings).
dhpak1.2:36.7: If I go with them, all will become weary and will be unable to obtain alms. I will send them on ahead.”
dhpak1.2:37.1: So he said to them: “Friends, you go on ahead.” – “But you, venerable Sir?”
dhpak1.2:37.2: – “I am weak, and on the way is a forest haunted by Amanussa.
dhpak1.2:37.3: If I go with you, you will all become weary; therefore you go on ahead.”
dhpak1.2:37.4: – “Do not so, venerable Sir; we will go only with you.”
dhpak1.2:37.5: – “Friends, please do not do so; if you do so, it will displease me.
dhpak1.2:37.6: When my younger brother sees you and asks after me, tell him that {1.14} I have lost the sight of my eyes, and he will send someone to guide my steps.
dhpak1.2:37.7: Greet in my name the One of Ten Strengths and the eighty great elders.” So saying, he dismissed them.
dhpak1.2:38.1: They begged the elder to pardon them for their insistence, and entered the village for alms.
dhpak1.2:38.2: The villagers provided them with seats, presented them with alms, and asked them: “Venerable Sirs, may we know why the noble bhikkhus are leaving?”
dhpak1.2:38.3: – “Yes, lay disciples, we desire to see the Teacher.”
dhpak1.2:38.4: The villagers repeatedly begged the bhikkhus to remain, but finding that they were firm in their determination to go,
dhpak1.2:38.5: accompanied them on their way weeping, and then turned back.
dhpak1.2:39.1: After journeying from place to place, the bhikkhus arrived at Jetavana and greeted the Teacher and the eighty great elders in the name of the elder.
dhpak1.2:39.2: Having done so, they entered the street where the elder’s younger brother lived for alms.
dhpak1.2:39.3: The householder recognized them, received them cordially, provided them with seats, and asked them:
dhpak1.2:39.4: “Where is my dear brother the elder?” They told him what had happened.
dhpak1.2:39.5: Flinging himself at their feet, he rolled on the ground and wept.
dhpak1.2:40.1: Then he asked them: “Now, friends, what is to be done?”
dhpak1.2:40.2: – “The elder wishes to have someone come from here, that he may return [28.154] with him.”
dhpak1.2:40.3: – “Friends, here is my sister’s son Pālita. Send him.” – “It will never do to send him, for there is danger by the way.
dhpak1.2:40.4: We might, however, send him, after first letting him go forth.” – “Do so, and then send him, friends.”
dhpak1.2:40.5: So they let him go forth and for a fortnight instructed him in such matters as the proper manner of putting on the robe.
dhpak1.2:40.6: Then, showing him the way, they sent him forth.
dhpak1.2:41.1: After journeying from place to place, he arrived at the village.
dhpak1.2:41.2: Seeing an old man at the village gate, he asked him: “Is there a forest hermitage near this village?”
dhpak1.2:41.3: – “There is, venerable Sir.” – “Who lives there?” – “An elder named Pālita, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.2:41.4: – “Show me the way there.” – “Who are you, venerable Sir?” – “I am the son of the elder’s sister.”
dhpak1.2:41.5: So the old man took him and {1.15} led him to the hermitage.
dhpak1.2:41.6: He worshipped the elder and for a fortnight performed the major and minor duties for him, ministering to him faithfully.
dhpak1.2:42.1: Then he said to him: “Venerable Sir, the householder, my mother’s brother, desires to have you come to him. Let us go there.”
dhpak1.2:42.2: – “Very well, take hold of my staff.” Taking hold of the staff by the tip, he entered the village with the elder.
dhpak1.2:42.3: The villagers provided the elder with a seat and asked him: “Venerable Sir, may we know your purpose in going?”
dhpak1.2:42.4: – “Yes, lay disciples, I am going to pay my respects to the Teacher.”
dhpak1.2:42.5: The villagers sought by all means in their power to persuade them to remain,
dhpak1.2:42.6: but failing in their efforts, escorted them part of the way, and then turned back weeping.
dhpak1.2:43.1: When the novice had gone part of the way with the elder, holding the tip of the elder’s staff,
dhpak1.2:43.2: he arrived at a forest village named Kaṭṭhanagara (Wood Town), near which the elder formerly resided.
dhpak1.2:43.3: As the novice came out of the village, he heard in the forest the voice of a woman singing away as she gathered firewood.
dhpak1.2:43.4: As he listened to her song, he fell in love with her voice.
dhpak1.2:44.1: There is no sound to be compared with a woman’s voice for power to thrill man’s whole frame.
dhpak1.2:44.2: Therefore said the Fortunate One: “Bhikkhus, I know of no other single sound which so completely takes possession of the heart of a man as this, bhikkhus;
dhpak1.2:44.3: namely, a woman’s voice.” The novice, fascinated by her voice, let go his hold of the elder’s staff.
dhpak1.2:44.4: He said: “Wait just a moment, venerable Sir; I have some business.”
dhpak1.2:44.5: So saying, {1.16} he went in the direction of the woman. When she saw him, she became silent.
dhpak1.2:44.6: The novice violated the law of [28.155] chastity with her.
dhpak1.2:44.7: The elder thought to himself: “Just now I heard the sound of someone singing, and it was none other than a woman’s voice.
dhpak1.2:44.8: The novice tarries; he must have violated the law of chastity.”
dhpak1.2:45.1: When the novice had finished his business, he returned to the elder and said: “Come, venerable Sir, let us be off.”
dhpak1.2:45.2: But the elder asked him: “Novice, have you done wrong?”
dhpak1.2:45.3: The novice remained silent, and though questioned repeatedly, answered never a word.
dhpak1.2:45.4: Then said the elder to him: “A wrongdoer like you can never hold the tip of my staff.”
dhpak1.2:46.1: The novice, overwhelmed with remorse, removed his yellow robes, clothed himself in the garb of a householder, and said:
dhpak1.2:46.2: “Venerable Sir, before I was a novice;
dhpak1.2:46.3: now I have become a lay disciple again.
dhpak1.2:46.4: It was not through faith that I went forth, but because I feared the dangers of the journey. Come, let us be off.”
dhpak1.2:47.1: The elder replied: “A wrongdoer is a wrongdoer, be he lay disciple or be he novice.
dhpak1.2:47.2: While you were a novice, you were unable to keep the law of chastity.
dhpak1.2:47.3: Will you be a better man for having become a lay disciple? A wrongdoer like you can never hold the tip of my staff.”
dhpak1.2:47.4: – “Venerable Sir, the road is infested with Amanussa and you are blind.
dhpak1.2:47.5: How can you remain here?” The elder answered: “Friend, don’t worry about that.
dhpak1.2:47.6: No matter whether I lie down right here and die, or wander here and there, with you I will never go.” So saying, he pronounced the following verses:
dhpak1.2:48.1: Alas! I have lost the sight of my eyes, across a desert I have come,
dhpak1.2:48.2: lying down and going no farther, with fools no fellowship may be. {1.17}
dhpak1.2:49.1: Alas! I have lost the sight of my eyes, across a desert I have come,
dhpak1.2:49.2: I will die and go no farther, with fools no fellowship may be.
dhpak1.2:50.1: When the novice heard this, he was overwhelmed with remorse.
dhpak1.2:50.2: And he cried out: “A grievous sin indeed have I committed, a deed of savagery and impropriety!”
dhpak1.2:50.3: And wringing his hands and weeping, he plunged into the forest and made off.
dhpak1.2:51.1: By the power of the elder’s virtue the Yellowstone Throne of Sakka, the Lord of the Devas,
dhpak1.2:51.2: sixty leagues long, fifty leagues wide, fifteen leagues thick, of the color of the China Rose flower,
dhpak1.2:51.3: which has a way of lowering itself when Sakka sits down and of rising again when he stands up, manifested signs of heat.
dhpak1.2:51.4: “Who, pray, can be seeking to thrust me from my seat?” thought Sakka.
dhpak1.2:51.5: Surveying the world with his Divine Eye, he saw the elder. Therefore those of old time said: [28.156]
dhpak1.2:52.1: The Lord of the Devas, the thousand-eyed, purified the Divine Eye
dhpak1.2:52.2: condemning wickedness, Pāla purified his livelihood.
dhpak1.2:53.1: The Lord of the Devas, the thousand-eyed, purified the Divine Eye
dhpak1.2:53.2: respecting the Dhamma, Pāla purified his livelihood.
dhpak1.2:54.1: Then this thought occurred to him: “Should I fail to go to the assistance of such a one,
dhpak1.2:54.2: who blamed wickedness, a Dhamma-revering elder,
dhpak1.2:54.3: my head is likely to split into seven pieces. I will go to him.” And so
dhpak1.2:55.1: The Lord of the Devas, the thousand-eyed, bearing glory in his sovereignty,
dhpak1.2:55.2: having approached in an instant, came close unto Cakkhupāla. {1.18}
dhpak1.2:56.1: Accordingly Sakka approached the elder. When he was quite near him, he shuffled his feet.
dhpak1.2:56.2: “Who is there?” asked the elder. “It is I, venerable Sir, a traveler.”
dhpak1.2:56.3: – “Where are you going, lay disciple?” – “To Sāvatthī, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.2:56.4: – “Continue your journey, friend.” – “But, venerable Sir, where is your reverence going?”
dhpak1.2:56.5: – “I am going there too.” – “Well then, let us go together, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.2:56.6: – “I am weak, friend. If you go with me, you will be delayed.” – “I have no urgent business.
dhpak1.2:56.7: Besides, if I go with you, I can avail myself of one of the ten ways and means of acquiring merit. Let us go together, venerable Sir.”
dhpak1.2:57.1: The elder thought to himself: “This is without doubt some pious man.”
dhpak1.2:57.2: So he said to him: “Very well, take hold of the tip of my staff, lay brother.”
dhpak1.2:57.3: Sakka did so. And Sakka shortened the distance so that they arrived at Jetavana at eventide.
dhpak1.2:57.4: The elder, hearing the noise of trumpets, drums, and other instruments of music, asked: “Where is that noise?”
dhpak1.2:57.5: – “At Sāvatthī, venerable Sir.” – “Lay brother, when I came here before, we were a long time in coming.”
dhpak1.2:57.6: – “I know a short cut, venerable Sir.” At that moment the elder perceived within himself: “This is no human being; it must be a Deva.”
dhpak1.2:58.1: The Lord of the Devas, the thousand-eyed, bearing glory in his sovereignty,
dhpak1.2:58.2: after having shortened the path, quickly came unto Sāvatthī.
dhpak1.2:59.1: Sakka conducted the elder to a hut of leaves and grass which his younger brother had made for his express use,
dhpak1.2:59.2: {1.19} seated him on a couch, and then, disguising himself as a dear friend of the younger brother, went to summon him.
dhpak1.2:59.3: “Friend Pāla!” he called out. “What is it, friend?”
dhpak1.2:59.4: – “Do you know that the elder has arrived?” – “No. Is it true that the elder has arrived?”
dhpak1.2:59.5: – “Yes, friend, I have just returned from the hermitage,
dhpak1.2:59.6: and saw the elder seated in the hut of leaves and grass you built for him.” So saying, he departed. [28.157]
dhpak1.2:60.1: The householder went to the hermitage. When he saw the elder, he flung himself at his feet, rolled on the ground, and wept.
dhpak1.2:60.2: Then he said: “I knew this would happen, venerable Sir.
dhpak1.2:60.3: It was for this reason that I withheld from you my permission to go forth.”
dhpak1.2:60.4: After talking with him for some time, he freed two slave-boys, had the elder let them go forth, and committed him to their care, saying:
dhpak1.2:60.5: “Bring rice porridge and other kinds of food from the village and minister to the elder.”
dhpak1.2:60.6: The novices ministered to the elder, performing the major and minor duties faithfully.
dhpak1.2:61.1: Now one day a party of bhikkhus residing in foreign parts came to Jetavana to see the Teacher.
dhpak1.2:61.2: After paying their respects to the Teacher and seeing the eighty great elders, they made the rounds of the monastery.
dhpak1.2:61.3: Coming to Cakkhupāla’s retreat, they said to each other: “Let us see him too.”
dhpak1.2:61.4: So when evening came, they set out to visit him. Just at that moment a severe storm arose.
dhpak1.2:61.5: So they turned back, saying: “It is now evening, and a storm has arisen.
dhpak1.2:61.6: Therefore we will go and see him in the morning.” The rain continued during the first watch, but ceased in the second.
dhpak1.2:61.7: The elder, a man of great energy, accustomed to walking, came down into the cloister in the last watch.
dhpak1.2:62.1: Now at that time many insects had come out of the newly wet earth, {1.20} and as the elder walked up and down, they perished in great numbers.
dhpak1.2:62.2: The resident bhikkhus did not sweep betimes where the elder walked.
dhpak1.2:62.3: When the visiting bhikkhus arrived, saying: “We would see the place where the elder resides,” and saw the insects in the cloister, they asked:
dhpak1.2:62.4: “Who was it that walked in this cloister?” – “Our master, venerable Sirs.”
dhpak1.2:62.5: They were offended and said: “See what the bhikkhu has done.
dhpak1.2:62.6: When he had the sight of his eyes, he lay down and slept and did no wrong.
dhpak1.2:62.7: But now that he has lost his eyesight, saying to himself: ‘I will take a walk,’ he has destroyed these insects.
dhpak1.2:62.8: ‘That which is right I will do,’ said he; but that which was not right he has done.”
dhpak1.2:63.1: So they went and reported the matter to the Realised One, saying: “Venerable Sir, the Elder Cakkhupāla, saying to himself:
dhpak1.2:63.2: ‘I will take a walk,’ has destroyed many insects.” – “But did you see him killing them?”
dhpak1.2:63.3: – “We did not, venerable Sir.” – “Precisely as you did not see him, so also did he not see these insects.
dhpak1.2:63.4: Bhikkhus, they who have destroyed the pollutants have no thought of killing.”
dhpak1.2:63.5: – “Venerable Sir, seeing that he was destined to become an Arahat, how was it that he became blind?”
dhpak1.2:63.6: – “Bhikkhus, it was by reason of his misdeed in a former existence.”
dhpak1.2:63.7: – “Why, venerable Sir, what did he do?” – “Well then, bhikkhus, listen.” [158]
dhpak1.2:64.2: The Wicked Physician and the Woman
dhpak1.2:65.1: In times long past, when the king of Kāsi reigned at Benāres, a certain physician went through towns and villages practicing his profession.
dhpak1.2:65.2: Seeing a certain woman with weak eyes, he asked her: “What is the matter with you?”
dhpak1.2:65.3: – “My eyesight has failed.” – “I will prescribe for you.”
dhpak1.2:65.4: – “Do so, master.” – “What will you give me?”
dhpak1.2:65.5: – “If you succeed in making my eyes well and strong again, I will become your slave, and my sons and daughters too.” – “Very well,” said he.
dhpak1.2:65.6: So he prescribed a remedy for her, and with a single application of the remedy her eyes became well and strong again. {1.21}
dhpak1.2:66.1: Upon this she thought: “I promised to become his slave, and my sons and daughters too.
dhpak1.2:66.2: But he will not treat me kindly. Therefore I will deceive him.”
dhpak1.2:66.3: So when the physician came and asked her how she was getting on, she answered: “Before, my eyes pained me a little; but now they hurt me worse than ever.”
dhpak1.2:66.4: The physician thought: “This woman is deceiving me because she is unwilling to give me anything.
dhpak1.2:66.5: I don’t want her fee; now I will make her blind.”
dhpak1.2:66.6: So he went home and told his wife about the matter. His wife said nothing.
dhpak1.2:66.7: Then he compounded an ointment, went to the woman’s house, and directed her to rub it into her eyes.
dhpak1.2:66.8: She did so, and her eyes went out like the flame of a lamp. That physician was Cakkhupāla.
dhpak1.2:67.1: “Bhikkhus, the wicked deed then committed by my son followed him ever after;
dhpak1.2:67.2: for a wicked deed follows the wrongdoer even as a wheel follows the hoof of the ox that bears the yoke.”
dhpak1.2:67.3: After relating this story, the Dhamma king joined the connection,
dhpak1.2:67.4: even as a king seals an edict with the royal seal after the clay has been affixed, and pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.2:68.2: manasā ce paduṭṭhena bhāsati vā karoti vā,
dhpak1.2:68.3: tato naṁ dukkham-anveti cakkaṁ va vahato padaṁ.
dhpak1.2:69.1: Mind precedes thoughts, mind is their chief, their quality is made by mind,
dhpak1.2:69.2: if with base mind one speaks or acts
dhpak1.2:69.3: through that, suffering follows one like a wheel follows ox’s foot.
dhpak1.2:70.1: At the end of the verse 30,000 bhikkhus became Arahats with the analytic knowledges.
dhpak1.2:70.2: This teaching that instilled fear was of benefit and fruitful to those assembled.
